deep.reconstruction:
The planet is CERES, not Pallas. The elements identify it: daily motion 770.858", log a = 0.44207 (a ≈ 2.767), φ ≈ 4°29.7' (e ≈ 0.0783), perihelion ≈ 146.5°, node ≈ 80°53', inclination ≈ 10°37.6'. The oppositions are spaced by about 463 days. 'Litt. S' and the later Jupiter line show this is Gauss's comparison of the Ceres oppositions of 1802–1808 with elliptic elements corrected for Jupiter perturbations.

(1) Table of observed oppositions (Paris mean time).
- Column 1: date.
- Column 2: t = days since the epoch 1802 Jan 0.0. Check: 31+28+17 = 76 days, and 3h45m11s = 0.15638 d, giving 76.15638. For 1803 July 1: 365+182 = 547 days, and 22h12m1s = 0.92501 d, giving 547.92502.
- Column 3: heliocentric longitude of Ceres at opposition, λ.
- Column 4: geocentric latitude β_geo.
- Columns 5–6: log R of the Earth's radius vector from two solar tables. The values are near 0, with minimum log at January perihelion and maximum at July aphelion.

(2) Elements and secular motions (per day). The epoch line most likely reads 1801.
- Mean longitude L_1801 = 77°20'5.26"; mean motion μ = 770.85842"/d; log μ = 2.8869746.
- L_1802 = L_1801 + 365μ = 77°20'5.26" + 281363.32" = 155°29'28.57" (verified).
- Perihelion ϖ = 146°29'53.76" + 0.33216"·t.
- φ = 4°29'41.95" − 0.003285"·t.
- log a = 0.4420728.
- Node Ω = 80°53'17.29" + 0.004052"·t.
- Inclination i = 10°37'35.45" + 0.0012"·t.
- The logs of the rates are written beside them.

(3) First opposition, t = 76.15638 (log 1.8817063).
- μt = 58705.79" = 16°18'25.79".
- Secular corrections: ϖ +25.30", φ −0.25", Ω +0.31", i +0.09".
- Corrected values: φ = 4°29'41.70"; ϖ = 146°30'19.06"; Ω = 80°53'17.60".
- Mean longitude L = 155°29'28.57" + 16°18'25.79" = 171°47'54.36".
- Mean anomaly M = L − ϖ = 25°17'35.30".
- Kepler's equation E − e"·sin E = M, with log e" = 4.2085786 (e" = 206264.8·sin φ ≈ 16157.7").
- Iteration: M + 2°3'48.28" gives E = 27°21'23.58". The log 9.6623105 is log sin E.
- True anomaly: v − E = 2°8'27.58", so v = 29°29'51.16". Equivalent to tan(v/2) = sqrt((1+e)/(1−e))·tan(E/2).
- Radius: log(1 − e cos E) = 9.9686669, so log r = 0.4420728 + 9.9686669 − 10 = 0.4107397. The 9.9843334½ is half this log, i.e. log sqrt(r/a) (my reading).
- Elliptic orbital longitude: ϖ + v = 176°0'10.22".

(4) Jupiter perturbation ('Litt. S').
- Jupiter's mean longitude: 142°50'34.9" + 6°19'50.8" = 149°10'25.7". Here 22790.8" = 76.156 × 299.26"/d, with log 2.4760530 = log of Jupiter's tropical daily motion.
- Ceres mean longitude 171°47'54.4".
- Argument L_Ceres − L_Jup = 22°37'29".
- Table terms: 315.15" + 629.86" = 945.01" = 15'45.01".
- The radius-vector perturbation is apparently −0.0039675 in log.
- Perturbed computed longitude in orbit: 176°0'10.22" + 15'45.01" = 176°15'55.23".

(5) Equation of condition. Gauss writes 176°15'55.23" + 87.708 dμ − 0.15168 dω + 1.15168 dE + 1.0?157 dφ. Here dE is the correction of the epoch mean longitude and dω the correction of the perihelion.
- ∂v/∂M = (1 + e cos v)²/(1 − e²)^{3/2} = 1.1517.
- So ∂/∂E = 1.15168, ∂/∂ϖ = 1 − 1.15168 = −0.15168, and ∂/∂μ = t·1.15168 = 87.708.
- ∂v/∂φ = sin v·(2 + e cos v)/cos φ ≈ 1.0216.

(6) Reduction of the observation to the orbit plane.
- λ − Ω = 176°21'29.5" − 80°53'17.60" = 95°28'11.90"; log tan = 1.0188...
- tan u = tan(λ − Ω)/cos i, with log cos i = 9.9924874, giving u = 95°22'36.19".
- Observed orbital longitude: u + Ω = 176°15'53.79". The residual is about −1.4".
- Heliocentric latitude: tan b = tan i·sin(λ − Ω), with logs 9.9980178 and 9.2732872. This gives b ≈ 10°34'45", written 10°34'45.10".
- The right-hand log columns (9.99866, 9.93733, 1.88171, 1.993856, 0.069606, 0.28427, 9.66231, 0.00925, ...) are an auxiliary computation. It is presumably the geocentric latitude from b, r and R at opposition; its details are not certain.

(7) Bottom lines: angles 170°7', 233°27', 43°34', 57°43', 256°5' and logs 1.96090, 9.83834, 3.45133, 9.85839n. These are presumably perturbation-table arguments and coefficients. Their purpose is unclear.

The next page repeats the same scheme for oppositions II–IV, producing one linear equation of condition per opposition. These are later to be solved, for example by least squares, for corrections to the elements.
errors: log 0.004052 = 7.60767, but Gauss writes 7.60763. The rate is probably 0.0040516 rounded, so the effect is negligible.
log 0.001200 = 7.07918, but Gauss writes 7.07941, i.e. a rate of 0.0012006. This too is a rounding of the written rate and negligible.

The dφ coefficient as transcribed (1.0457) does not match theory, which gives ∂v/∂φ ≈ 1.0216. The overwritten digit is probably meant as 1.02157, so this is a reading issue rather than a computational error.

Heliocentric latitude: my recomputation from the given logs gives about 10°34'47" against Gauss's 10°34'45.10". This is a difference of a couple of arcseconds and within reading uncertainty of the logs.
No substantive arithmetic errors were found. The sums and differences of angles (L, M, E, v, ϖ+v, λ−Ω, u+Ω) all check exactly.

results.what: Reduction of six Ceres oppositions (1802–1808) to heliocentric longitude and latitude and Earth's log R
Elliptic place from mean elements with secular motions: Kepler's equation by iteration, then true anomaly and radius vector
results.modern_name: Solution of Kepler's equation / two-body ephemeris

results.what: Addition of Jupiter's perturbations to Ceres' longitude from his tables (Litt. S), with argument L_Ceres − L_Jup
results.modern_name: Special/general perturbation tables (first-order Jupiter perturbations of Ceres)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's own Ceres perturbation work c. 1802–1812

results.what: Linear equations of condition for corrections of the elements: coefficients t·dv/dM, 1−dv/dM, dv/dM, dv/dφ
results.modern_name: Differential correction of orbital elements (precursor of least-squares orbit fitting)

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine working material from Gauss's well-documented Ceres orbit and perturbation computations. It sets up equations of condition from successive oppositions, which is known practice of his. No new mathematics appears.

checkable.asserts: Epoch 1801 to 1802 mean longitude increment is 365 days of mean motion
E = 27°21'23.58" solves Kepler's equation for M = 25°17'35.30"
dφ coefficient is about 1.0216 (suggests the reading 1.02157)
Argument of latitude u = 95°22'36.19" from λ−Ω and i

transcription_corrections: The planet symbol is Ceres (Gauss's sickle sign ⚳), not Pallas ⚴. The elements (n = 770.86"/d, e ≈ 0.078, Ω ≈ 80°53', i ≈ 10°37') are those of Ceres.
The heading likely reads 'Vergleichung der 6 Oppositionen' or similar; six oppositions are listed.
The epoch line should read 'Epoche 1801 Paris 77°20'5.26"'. The 1802 value is 365 days of motion later.
The dφ coefficient '1,0457' is probably 1,02157, overwritten.
'♂ 22.37.29' is the difference of mean longitudes Ceres − Jupiter, not Mars.
